title: Yehoshua the Man
subtitle: A Sacred Encounter in Word and Orchestra
welcome: This suite invites you into a living encounter with Yehoshua — not a doctrine about Him, but a meeting with Him. Narrator and orchestra together introduce us to aspects of His personal character. There is nothing required of you except to listen.
closingReflection: What manner of man is this?

movements.title: Invocation
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to the first movement — Humility.
movements.teaser: A single oboe voice draws the listener from the dust and duty of daily life to a doorway — and a question that opens the whole suite.
movements.emotionalArc: The listener enters a world of ordinary motion — the persistent press of daily life — and is drawn by a searching oboe melody toward a threshold. The arc moves from restless distraction to the stillness of a doorway, closing with a whispered question that the remaining nine movements will answer.
movements.programNote: The suite opens where the manuscript opens — not in a sanctuary, but on a dirt road, where every household is already in motion. The solo oboe sounds the Invocation leitmotif that will recur as the suite's musical signature: a melodic question threading through the movements that follow. Five scenes carry the listener from the dust and duty of daily life, through the Bethany house where Mary chose to sit at His feet while Martha served, to the quiet challenge of Joshua's ancient summons. The movement does not resolve the choice it presents. It opens the door and delivers its final question — 'What manner of man is this?' — as a whisper into silence.

movements.title: Humility
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to Obedience.
movements.teaser: The quietest movement in the suite — a solo cello that never announces itself, because humility can't.
movements.emotionalArc: The music withdraws into the most intimate register of the suite. The solo cello speaks quietly throughout — this is not the silence of emptiness but the presence of a person who does not need the room to know they are there. The arc moves through three decades of quiet labor, a deflection of glory to the Father, and an entry into Jerusalem on a borrowed donkey.
movements.programNote: The quietest movement in the suite is not quiet by accident. The cello that carries it never announces itself. It speaks and then waits, playing phrases that refuse self-display — which is itself the musical enactment of what the movement describes. This is Yehoshua who spent thirty years shaping wood and stone before He ever shaped souls publicly. This is the teacher who answered a young man's question about eternal life by redirecting all glory to the Father. Paul named it precisely: He made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant. The leitmotif is entirely absent here — a choice with its own meaning. Humility cannot summon attention to itself. It simply serves and moves on.
movements.beatitude: Blessed are the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3)

movements.title: Obedience
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to Compassion.
movements.teaser: Obedience, expected to feel heavy, arrives as relief — the moment the yoke fits and the burden becomes, somehow, light.
movements.emotionalArc: The listener's expectation is deliberately inverted. The arc moves from the young son learning carpentry in Nazareth, through the extraordinary moment He walked away from a crowd wanting to crown Him king, arriving at the central image of the yoke that fits perfectly — the burden carried not alone but in partnership.
movements.programNote: This movement is built on an inversion the manuscript names directly: obedience does not feel like constraint — it feels like relief. The E♭ major key, a half-step rise from the suite's D home, opens into brightness and space. Strings and woodwinds carry an easy, unhurried walking pulse — not a march, but the gait of someone who has put down a heavy load and found the path ahead suddenly clear. The movement's heart is a moment the manuscript describes as God saying within: Let there be light. The yoke is not taken up with dread. It fits. And the burden — borne together with the One who designed it — is, miraculously, light.
movements.beatitude: Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness (Matthew 5:6)

movements.title: Compassion
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to Teaching.
movements.teaser: A movement that enters grief honestly and does not leave it quickly — the most carefully produced silence in the suite follows two words.
movements.emotionalArc: The movement enters grief honestly and does not leave it quickly. The cello descends into it alone. Over four scenes the music moves from a leper's broken plea through the mourning at Lazarus's tomb, arriving at the most restrained moment of the suite. The silence that follows those two words is not absence — it is presence. Then: resurrection.
movements.programNote: The central moment of this movement is a silence no instrument can generate — it must be built by hand, in the edit. After the narrator speaks the two words 'Jesus wept,' both the music and the voice cease completely. What the listener experiences in that silence is the heart of the movement: not absence, but the presence of a Savior who chose to walk the full distance of human grief rather than heal from a safe distance. The Greek word the manuscript offers — splagchnizomai — describes being shaken to the core by another's suffering and then moving to act. The cello that carries this movement is the voice of that shaking. When the music returns, it returns with full strings — because grief that has been entered and shared does not remain in the minor key.

movements.title: Teaching
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to Meekness and Courage.
movements.teaser: Three woodwind voices in unhurried conversation — the musical form of a teacher who calibrated every method to the soul standing before Him.
movements.emotionalArc: The listener sits down at the well. An unhurried, guileless conversation unfolds between woodwind voices — question answered by question, curiosity drawn forward by curiosity. The arc moves from sparse opening through four teaching methods revealed in full warmth, to an intimate close as the narrator reflects personally.
movements.programNote: G major is the tonality of guilelessness — harmonically clear, nothing hidden, no accidentals that don't belong. It is the right key for this movement, because the manuscript's governing Beatitude is pure in heart. The woodwind voices trade phrases the way a great teacher trades questions with a willing student: one asks, another answers, a third opens what was just closed. The well scene in John 4 is the chamber through which this movement passes — a Samaritan woman who came at noon to avoid her peers, and the rabbi who waited there and asked her for a drink. What the manuscript traces is the pattern beneath every encounter: parables for crowds, direct doctrine for disciples, piercing questions for the powerful, silence for those with no interest in the answer. Every method was an act of grace calibrated to the soul standing before Him.
movements.beatitude: Blessed are the pure in heart (Matthew 5:8)

movements.title: Meekness and Courage
movements.graceLabel: The Meekness and Courage of Yehoshua
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to Justice and Mercy.
movements.teaser: The same hands appear in both scenes — and the movement makes the listener hold both before giving the resolution.
movements.emotionalArc: The suite's most structurally unstable movement holds two seemingly opposite scenes in tension throughout. The oboe descends to its most intimate register at the foot-washing; the brass rises to the suite's loudest moment at the temple cleansing. The final scene brings both into a single resolved declaration: not contradiction, but mastery.
movements.programNote: The same hands appear in both scenes. They washed feet in the upper room. They made a whip of cords in the temple court. The manuscript's governing declaration is the movement's musical thesis: meekness is not weakness, courage is not rage. To carry both scenes in the same movement is an architectural choice — the listener must hold them together before the resolution is given. The leitmotif echoes here for only the second time in the suite, surfacing quietly in the solo oboe at the moment the manuscript names as the deepest act of meekness: the Master kneeling before the disciple who will deny Him. The brass arrives later — measured, premeditated, not sudden — because the temple cleansing was not an outburst. He found a place where He could sit down. And He made a whip of cords.
movements.beatitude: Blessed are the meek · Blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:5, 9)

movements.title: Justice and Mercy
movements.graceLabel: The Justice and Mercy of Yehoshua
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to Joy.
movements.teaser: A courtroom that becomes a clearing — the most dramatic silence in the suite, then eight words from a single violin.
movements.emotionalArc: The suite travels furthest from its tonal home here. The movement opens under the weight of accusation, builds to a crowd on the edge of verdict, falls into its most dramatically constructed silence, and arrives — from that silence — into the warmth of a single violin and eight words spoken to one person in a clearing.
movements.programNote: The governing image the manuscript offers is a courtroom that becomes a clearing. Low brass carry the weight of measured reckoning through the first half — this is not rage, but the settled authority of the Woes: judgment, and mercy, and faith. The movement's most carefully constructed moment is the silence after the crowd departs — a hard cut in both music and narration, dead air, and then a single violin entering from stillness. That violin carries everything that follows: Neither do I condemn thee. The movement that opened under the heaviest brass in the suite closes on an open, unresolved violin harmonic — because the commission 'go and sin no more' points forward, not backward.

movements.title: Joy
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to the Beatitudes.
movements.teaser: The tempo peak of the suite — upper strings and flute airborne from the opening bar, because this is the kind of man who made rooms feel different.
movements.emotionalArc: The suite reaches its tempo peak. Upper strings and flute are present from the first bar. The arc moves from the wedding at Cana through the interior source of joy in Luke 10:21, arriving at the suite's most radiant moment: the risen Lord weeping over children not from sorrow but from grace overflowing. A single voice closes with a personal invitation.
movements.programNote: His enemies meant it as an insult. The manuscript receives it as a description: a man who showed up at feasts, turned water into wine at a wedding, and drew the accusation of being a friend of tax collectors and sinners. A major is the suite's dominant key — one step from the D major home — and the gravitational pull toward resolution is already in motion. The leitmotif surfaces for the last time before the Beatitudes in the solo flute: recognition, not announcement, in the scene where Jesus rejoiced in spirit at the Father's work bearing fruit. The movement's emotional summit is a scene where the risen Lord kneels among children, weeping not from sorrow but from joy so full it overflowed. This is the manuscript's definition of joy: not the absence of sorrow, but a gladness so deep it survives grief.
movements.beatitude: Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake (Matthew 5:10)

movements.title: Beatitudes
movements.interstitial: The suite now turns to its close — the Benediction.
movements.teaser: Eight Beatitudes spoken as theme-and-variations — then the suite's central revelation, arrived at with full orchestra.
movements.emotionalArc: The suite returns home — to D major and to the Invocation leitmotif in full statement for the first time since Movement I. The Beatitudes are spoken one by one, each one a movement in miniature. At the apex, the central revelation of the chapter arrives with full orchestral weight, then falls to near-silence: He not only described what His disciples should become — He described what He already was.
movements.programNote: The entire suite has been building toward this moment. The Beatitudes, spoken one by one through the first half of the movement, are not instructions being reviewed — they are character traits being recognized, because the listener has just spent seven movements meeting the person who already embodies each one. Poor in spirit: the cello that refused to announce itself. They that mourn: the man who wept beside a tomb. Pure in heart: the teacher at the well with nothing hidden. The full orchestra enters the movement's apex at the central revelation — the manuscript's own theological turning point — and then withdraws to near-silence for a pause the music cannot fill. The suite's tonal journey resolves to D major here. The movement closes on an open harmonic, pointing forward — because the Benediction has not yet spoken.

movements.title: Benediction
movements.teaser: The suite does not end by arriving — it ends by departing, the music thinning to a single cello until only silence remains.
movements.emotionalArc: Five brief scenes address the listener directly from the words of John 17, spoken over music that is already withdrawing. The oboe and cello — the suite's two solo voices — sound together only once in the entire work, here, before the oboe hands the final phrase to the cello alone. The suite ends when the cello decides.
movements.programNote: A concert typically ends with the finale — the fullest, loudest, most triumphant statement. This movement is the deliberate opposite of that. The manuscript's Benediction is an address, not a climax. Each of its five movements — He saw you, It has already begun in you, His arms are open wide, His hands will bless you, His voice calls you home — is spoken over music that thins a little further with each phrase, as if the encounter is gently receding and leaving something behind. The oboe and cello — the suite's two primary solo voices — sound together only once in the entire work, here, in the final third of the final movement. Then the oboe hands the last phrase of the leitmotif to the cello alone. The suite ends in near-silence. The listener is sent.
